title: Equal Fractions
author: TextSavvy
summary: This Learning & Curriculum piece is part of an ongoing series on teaching fractions, and it tackles the philosophical question of whether mathematics is invented or discovered as a lens for teaching equal fractions. The author rejects the common instructional framing that separates arbitrary convention from logically derived consequence, arguing instead that mathematics is best understood as an invented language of patterns rather than a fixed truth waiting to be uncovered. From that premise, the piece builds a concrete classroom explanation of why fractions like one-half and two-fourths are equal, using a 'multiply the whole universe of half-apples' thought experiment and diagrams to make the underlying multiplicative structure visible to students. The author also argues for embracing rough, handwritten diagrams over pristine, authoritative-looking ones, on the grounds that presenting mathematics as a human, revisable language rather than a sacred script may reduce students' fear of manipulating equations. The essay closes by positioning equal fractions as a pivotal 'handoff point' in a longer curricular sequence leading toward understanding fractions as division statements.
points: Argues that treating mathematics as either purely invented or purely discovered is a false binary that distracts from actual instructional design questions.
Builds the equal-fractions concept from a concrete multiplicative model (converting a whole universe of halves into fourths) rather than starting from an abstract rule.
Advocates for scruffy, handwritten diagrams over polished ones, arguing this reduces students' fear of writing unconventional but valid equalities like 4/6 = 2/3.
Frames equal fractions as a deliberate 'handoff point' toward teaching fractions as division statements later in the sequence, not an isolated topic.
quotes: There is a longstanding conversation amongst some in education about when it is appropriate to flat-out tell students things and when it is better to expect them to reason instead.
My view on this undecided philosophical question is that it is all invented.
When the numerator and denominator of a fraction are each multiplied or divided by the same number, the resulting numerator and denominator form another, equal, fraction.
Mathematics should be seen as a scruffy language humans scribble and erase when trying to describe perfection, not as a language of the gods that one must copy so as to instantiate it.
There are good reasons, it seems to me, for using equal fractions as the handoff point for developing the story of fractions as division statements.
